title: Metrics, KRIs, and Reporting
objective: By the end of this lesson you can distinguish metrics from KRIs, read trend direction, name AI-specific KRIs, and shape a report for executives.

blocks.text: Metrics measure activity; KRIs warn about risk

A metric is any measured value: number of patches applied, MFA coverage, training completion. A key risk indicator (KRI) is a metric chosen because it moves ahead of, or with, a risk the organization cares about. Rising phishing click rates, growing numbers of unremediated critical vulnerabilities, and falling patch compliance are KRIs: when they move in the wrong direction, loss events become more likely.

rows: Metric (and a KRI when tracked against a threshold)
Directly reflects control coverage for account-takeover risk
Phishing simulation click rate rising for 3 campaigns
Leading signal that account compromise likelihood is rising
Critical vulnerabilities open longer than 30 days doubling
Exposure window for exploitation is widening
Activity count; says nothing about risk change

blocks.text: Direction and thresholds are what make indicators useful. A KRI is defined with a green-amber-red threshold and an owner who reacts when the line crosses into amber. An indicator without a threshold is just a number on a chart.
The 2026 outline adds AI-specific key risk indicators because AI use is now a governance concern. Think of them as KRIs for a new class of exposure.

items: Sensitive data found in prompts to public AI services (leakage exposure).
Number of AI tools or models in use without security review (shadow AI).
Model performance or drift alerts unresolved beyond threshold (decision quality risk).
AI-related incidents or near misses reported per quarter.
Share of AI systems with logged, traceable actions and defined owners.

blocks.text: Executives need decisions and comparisons, not tool output. A good security report leads with risk posture and trend, states what changed since last period, flags items needing a decision, and translates technical counts into business exposure. The audience-shaping rule: for executives, lead with risk and decisions; for practitioners, include the technical detail in an appendix.

items: Lead with: overall posture, movement of key KRIs, incidents and their business impact.
Then: compliance status, budget-relevant findings, decisions requested with options.
Appendix: detailed metrics, tool outputs, technical evidence.
Cadence: brief and frequent beats long and rare; align reporting to governance meetings.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Two patterns repeat. First, pick the KRI over the raw activity count: risk-linked and thresholded beats volume-of-work. Second, pick the report that matches its audience: risk language and decisions for the board, technical depth for the SOC.

blocks.title: Build a KRI line
steps: Pick one risk your organization (or a fictional shop) cares about, such as account compromise.
Choose one metric that moves with that risk and define an amber and red threshold for it.
Write the one-sentence escalation: who is told and what they decide when red is hit.
blocks.expected: Example: risk = account compromise. KRI = percentage of privileged accounts without MFA. Amber above 5%, red above 10%. On red, the CISO pauses new access grants until coverage is restored.

cheatsheet: Metric = measurement; KRI = metric tied to a risk, with thresholds and an owner.
Good KRIs: phishing click rate trend, unremediated critical vulnerabilities, MFA coverage gap, patch compliance slide.
AI-specific KRIs: sensitive data in public AI prompts, unreviewed AI tools (shadow AI), unresolved model drift, AI incidents, traceability coverage.
Executive reports lead with risk posture, trends, and decisions requested; technical detail goes to appendices.
An indicator without a threshold and owner is decoration.

checkpoint.prompt: Which of these is the strongest KRI for ransomware exposure?

choices.A: Count of critical vulnerabilities older than 30 days, trending upward
choices.B: Number of security awareness emails sent this quarter
choices.C: Number of firewall rules in place
choices.D: Total pages of the security policy set

checkpoint.explanation: Aging critical vulnerabilities widen the exploitation window for ransomware entry, and the upward trend signals rising risk: that is a KRI. Email counts, rule counts, and page counts are activity or inventory, not risk-linked indicators.

checkpoint.prompt: You must brief the board on security. Your opening slide should present:

choices.A: Raw SIEM alert counts by product
choices.B: The full list of firewall rule changes
choices.C: Risk posture, KRI trends, and decisions requested

checkpoint.explanation: Boards govern risk, so the report leads with posture, trend, and decisions needed. Operational detail supports the story in appendices, not the opening.
